thinking_and_logic: The implemented approach scans the array and collects indices where nums[i] equals target. This does not address the Two Sum requirement, which is to find two distinct indices whose values sum to target. The failures across basic cases (including two elements, pair at end, duplicates, negatives) are consistent with this mismatch rather than isolated edge-case handling.
code_assessment: Compared to the answer key, the final code misses the key technique entirely: checking complements using a hash map (seen value -> index) in a single pass. The optimal approach returns as soon as it finds target - nums[i] already seen, guaranteeing two distinct indices and O(n) time. The submitted code never considers pairs, never checks complements, and can return any number of indices (including 0 or >2), so it cannot satisfy the problem’s contract.

next_steps.action: Re-solve Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (complement check before insert).
next_steps.why: It is the canonical O(n) solution and directly enforces the 'two distinct indices whose sum is target' requirement.
next_steps.how: Maintain dict seen = {value: index}. For each index i, compute c = target - nums[i]. If c in seen, return [seen[c], i]. Otherwise set seen[nums[i]] = i.

next_steps.action: Adopt a 60-second pre-coding validation habit (restate + one manual example).
next_steps.why: This prevents fundamental misreads like searching for nums[i] == target instead of a pair sum.
next_steps.how: Before writing code, write down: 'need i!=j and nums[i]+nums[j]=target; exactly one answer'. Then run through [2,7,11,15], 9 and confirm your planned logic returns [0,1].

next_steps.action: Practice variants to reinforce the pattern boundary (sorted array -> two pointers).
next_steps.why: It builds intuition for when to use hashing vs two pointers and how to keep indices straight.
next_steps.how: Solve: (1) unsorted -> hash map; (2) sorted -> two pointers; (3) return values vs indices; (4) handle duplicates carefully.
